question: Can independently trained neural networks be moved into a common low-loss linear region by applying function-preserving hidden-unit permutations, and can that alignment make weight averaging useful?

key_findings.claim: The paper contributes three concrete permutation-search methods, of which data-free weight matching is the practically important result.
key_findings.evidence: Activation matching solves an independent linear assignment from cross-model activations at each layer; weight matching approximately maximizes the global parameter inner product by repeated layerwise assignment updates; and the straight-through estimator minimizes midpoint loss while projecting onto realizable permutations. Across the selected MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet pairs, the straight-through method is best but expensive, while weight matching is close and runs in seconds to minutes without data.

key_findings.claim: Permutation alignment sharply reduces interpolation barriers, including essentially zero reported barriers for sufficiently wide ResNet20 models on CIFAR-10, but the evidence is pairwise and architecture-dependent rather than a demonstration of one global basin.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 2 reports zero-barrier MNIST interpolation after all three matching methods and a 67% ImageNet barrier reduction rather than elimination. Figure 4 shows the matched train and test barriers decreasing with width, reaching approximately zero only for the widest ResNet20 setting. The experiments use selected pairs of endpoints; they do not establish that arbitrary pairs, triples, or all SGD solutions share a convex set.

anchors.section: Loss Landscapes Before and After Matching / Figure 4

key_findings.claim: Linear mode connectivity in these experiments emerges during training and improves with width, but the causal attribution to permutation availability remains unresolved.
key_findings.evidence: For three-layer MLPs on MNIST and CIFAR-10, Figure 3 shows barriers falling over epochs rather than being absent at initialization. For VGG16 and ResNet20 on CIFAR-10, Figure 4 shows lower matched barriers as width increases. The authors explicitly leave open whether thin-model failures reflect a deficient search method or invariances beyond permutation; later work also finds width can enable connectivity without permutation after calibration.

key_findings.claim: The finite counterexample correctly blocks any architecture-only or universal version of the linear-connectivity claim.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix A.6 constructs two two-hidden-layer ReLU networks that realize the same two-dimensional classifier while all four function-preserving hidden-unit permutations exhibit a barrier on their linear interpolation. The construction is not an SGD counterexample, but it shows that architecture and permutation symmetry alone cannot imply linear mode connectivity; an optimizer-dependent restriction is essential.

anchors.section: A Counterexample to Universal Linear Mode Connectivity

key_findings.claim: The split-data experiment shows a useful loss and calibration effect, not competitive task recovery or a validated privacy-preserving federated-learning method.
key_findings.evidence: Two ResNet20 models trained on oppositely biased CIFAR-100 subsets are aligned without data and averaged. The midpoint improves test loss relative to either endpoint and has a better-looking reliability diagram, but it remains worse than full-data training and a two-model ensemble, and Figure 10 shows that its top-1 accuracy is not competitive. No privacy attack, client-scale federation, heterogeneous architecture, communication analysis, ECE, Brier score, or uncertainty is reported.

anchors.section: Model Patching, Split Data Training, and Improved Calibration / Figure 5

key_findings.claim: MergeMany lowers held-out cross-entropy in the reported MNIST example but slightly lowers accuracy, and the paper mislabels an ordinary test split as out-of-distribution performance.
key_findings.evidence: For five MLPs, Table 3 reports individual test losses from 0.1108 to 0.1531 and accuracies from 98.54% to 98.71%; the merged model has lower test loss 0.0727 but lower accuracy 98.31%. The caption calls this better out-of-distribution performance even though it is the standard MNIST test set from the same benchmark distribution. The 32-model calibration plot is a separate selected run without repeated-group uncertainty.

key_findings.claim: The ImageNet path is not a strictly linear path in the complete deployed-model state because BatchNorm statistics are recomputed after interpolation.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix A.3.3 states that BatchNorm statistics are recalculated after weight interpolation, following advice received after initial publication; Appendix A.4 recommends this because interpolation causes variance collapse. Thus the reported ImageNet curve combines linear trainable-weight interpolation with a data-dependent nonlinear update of running statistics. It is valid as a repair pipeline, but it is not direct evidence that the two full parameter-and-buffer states lie on one linear low-loss segment.

anchors.section: Appendix A.3.3 / ResNet50 Models on ImageNet-1K

key_findings.claim: The stated approximation-hardness result for bilinear assignment is not established by the supplied reduction.
key_findings.evidence: Lemma 1 is described in the main text as admitting no polynomial-time constant-factor approximation scheme, while Appendix A.12 concludes only that the problem has no PTAS. More importantly, the reduction enforces P=Q by adding lambda-dependent terms and leaves the QAP objective plus a potentially dominant additive constant. Such an additive shift does not preserve multiplicative approximation ratios, especially for an objective allowed to be negative. The construction supports exact NP-hardness but does not by itself transfer the cited inapproximability result.

key_findings.claim: The termination proof for Algorithm 1 silently assumes strict-improvement tie handling that the pseudocode does not specify.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix A.13 asserts that every permutation-changing layer update strictly increases the global inner-product utility. A linear assignment can instead have multiple equal optima, permitting a permutation change with equal utility. The released implementation does terminate because it only marks progress on an improvement larger than 1e-12 and stops after a pass with no such progress, even though it still installs tied assignments. The mathematical pseudocode and proof need the same strict acceptance or deterministic tie rule.

key_findings.claim: The empirical study is broad for its time but mostly reports selected endpoint pairs without statistical uncertainty or exhaustive controls.
key_findings.evidence: Figures 2-5 and 8-13 generally show one pair or one group of trained models, curves without confidence intervals, and no stated number of independent endpoint-pair draws. Width, optimizer, normalization, schedule, and architecture differ across experiments; the paper lists several failures but does not estimate their frequency. Calibration is assessed visually rather than with scalar metrics, and no hypothesis test supports the language of a single basin.

key_findings.claim: The author artifact exposes the core algorithms and experiment scripts, but end-to-end reproduction is substantially less turnkey than the paper's reproducibility statement suggests.
key_findings.evidence: The MIT-licensed repository contains JAX implementations, architecture-specific permutation specifications, training and plotting scripts, a pinned 2022 Nix environment, and W&B project references; the public head inspected was ef40098257ab97243930eba737d6dcb8edd5863e. It has no experiment command guide beyond the abstract, no manifest mapping figures to runs, no CI, no packaged tests, no release, and no locally bundled checkpoints or result tables. Many scripts fetch named W&B artifacts, making the external project state part of the reproduction path. A public third-party one-click audit reported failure to reproduce the key barrier result, which is a warning rather than a peer-reviewed refutation.

method.core_idea: Quotient neural-network parameter space by hidden-unit permutations, choose a representative of one trained model that aligns with another, and average or interpolate only after this re-basing step.
method.mechanism: Activation matching forms cross-model activation Gram matrices and solves one Hungarian assignment per layer. Weight matching instead maximizes the inner product between one model and a permuted copy of the other; because the coupled sum of bilinear assignments is hard, it repeatedly optimizes one layer permutation while holding all others fixed. The straight-through method keeps unconstrained proxy weights, projects them onto a realizable permutation of the second endpoint with weight matching in the forward pass, and differentiates midpoint loss through the unprojected proxy. MergeMany cyclically aligns each model to the mean of all other current models before averaging all aligned weights.
assumptions: Models being merged share an architecture and compatible tensor shapes.
All chosen permutations preserve the network function, including tied channel permutations across residual branches and normalization parameters.
A useful alignment lies within discrete hidden-unit permutation symmetries; scaling, sign, rotation, cross-layer, and more general linear symmetries are mostly excluded.
Activation matching has access to representative input data and its learned activation statistics transfer to evaluation data.
Weight-space proximity is a useful surrogate for a low-loss interpolation even though the matching objective contains no task loss.
The layerwise coordinate search reaches a useful local optimum from the identity initialization.
Endpoint training uses SGD-like procedures whose implicit bias favors alignable solutions; the finite counterexample shows arbitrary solutions need not be alignable.
Sufficient overparameterization, especially width, is available for the tested zero-barrier cases.
BatchNorm running statistics may be recomputed from data at interpolated points, changing the strict full-state linear-path interpretation.
Loss and top-1 accuracy along a finite interpolation grid adequately measure the barrier.
Reliability diagrams without scalar calibration summaries are sufficient for the reported calibration conclusions.
Pairwise alignment can be extended to many models by repeated alignment to their current mean.

techniques.role: Aligns hidden units by solving linear assignments that minimize squared disagreement between their dataset activations.
Greedily maximizes the whole-model cross-parameter inner product over function-preserving channel permutations.
Turns each layer-coordinate update into an exactly solvable Hungarian linear assignment.
Optimizes midpoint task loss through a discrete permutation projection with a straight-through gradient.
Encodes which parameter axes must share a permutation across dense, convolutional, residual, and normalization structures.
Evaluates train and test loss or accuracy across a grid of linear interpolation coefficients.
Measures how post-alignment barriers change as VGG16 and ResNet20 channel widths increase.
Tests data-free alignment and averaging of models trained on oppositely biased CIFAR-100 subsets.
Iteratively aligns each of several models to the mean of the remaining models before parameter averaging.
Recomputes BatchNorm statistics after interpolation to mitigate activation-variance collapse in ImageNet experiments.
Constructs equal-function endpoints for which no hidden-unit permutation yields a barrier-free linear path.

evaluations.setting: Three-hidden-layer, width-512 MLPs trained independently on MNIST
evaluations.metric: Train and test loss barrier along matched interpolation
evaluations.result: All three matching methods report an approximately zero barrier; weight and straight-through matching also yield a midpoint with lower test loss than both endpoints.
evaluations.baseline: Naive interpolation has a large midpoint loss spike.

evaluations.setting: VGG16 and ResNet20 width sweep on CIFAR-10
evaluations.metric: Train and test loss barrier after weight matching
evaluations.result: Barriers decrease with width; the widest reported ResNet20 at 32x reaches approximately zero train and test barrier.
evaluations.baseline: One-times-width models retain substantial barriers; 8x VGG16 could not be trained because of GPU memory.

evaluations.setting: Two independently trained ResNet50 models on ImageNet-1K, with BatchNorm statistics recalculated after interpolation
evaluations.metric: Loss barrier and midpoint top-1 accuracy
evaluations.result: Weight matching reduces the reported loss barrier by 67%; the appendix reports 51.01% midpoint top-1 accuracy.
evaluations.baseline: Naive averaging collapses; OT-Fusion reaches 1.38% midpoint top-1 accuracy in the authors' implementation.

evaluations.setting: Published VGG11/CIFAR-10 endpoints from Singh and Jaggi
evaluations.metric: Merged-model test accuracy and matching runtime
evaluations.result: Weight matching obtains 86.57% test accuracy in 0.64 seconds.

evaluations.setting: ResNet20 models trained on oppositely biased, disjoint CIFAR-100 subsets
evaluations.metric: Combined-distribution test loss, top-1 accuracy, and reliability diagrams
evaluations.result: The aligned midpoint has lower test loss and visibly better calibration than either input, but its top-1 accuracy is not competitive.
evaluations.baseline: It beats naive weight averaging but trails full-data training and a two-model logit ensemble.

evaluations.setting: MergeMany applied to five independently trained MNIST MLPs
evaluations.result: Merged test loss is 0.0727 versus 0.1108-0.1531 for individual models; merged accuracy is 98.31% versus 98.54%-98.71% individually.
evaluations.baseline: The model improves cross-entropy but not accuracy over any endpoint.

evaluations.setting: MergeMany applied to 32 MNIST MLPs, each trained on a random 50% subset
evaluations.result: The merged model's plotted calibration approaches the ensemble while using one model at inference.
evaluations.baseline: Naive averaging collapses; the 32-model ensemble uses 32 times the inference memory and compute.

evaluations.setting: Algorithm 1 wall-clock audit on an AWS p3.2xlarge with NVIDIA V100
evaluations.result: 3 seconds for a 3x512 MLP, 33 seconds for ResNet50, and 194 seconds for 32x-width ResNet20.
evaluations.baseline: The straight-through alternative requires a conventional task-loss training loop and is described as much more expensive.

evaluations.setting: Two-hidden-layer, two-unit ReLU counterexample on a synthetic quadrant classification task
evaluations.metric: Barrier across every function-preserving unit permutation
evaluations.result: All four possible alignments retain a barrier despite both endpoints fitting the task perfectly.
evaluations.baseline: This rules out universal architecture-only connectivity but does not test SGD-generated endpoints.

limitations: Author-stated: the methods fail for insufficiently wide models, early training, VGGs on MNIST, certain optimizer-learning-rate combinations, and ConvNeXt architectures with few useful channel permutations.
Author-stated: permutation symmetry is only part of the invariance structure; scaling, cross-layer movement, and general linear activation relations are not handled.
Author-stated: failure to find a permutation cannot disprove that a satisfactory one exists because the search space is enormous.
Author-stated: 8x VGG16 was infeasible on the available GPU, limiting the clean width trend for that family.
Reviewer-identified: the evidence consists primarily of selected model pairs or model groups, with no pair-sampling protocol, repeated-run distribution, confidence interval, or failure frequency.
Reviewer-identified: the phrase single basin is stronger than pairwise low-barrier line segments; pairwise connectivity does not establish one jointly convex region containing all aligned solutions.
Reviewer-identified: ImageNet BatchNorm-statistic recalculation makes the evaluated path data-dependent and not linear in the full deployed state.
Reviewer-identified: calibration claims rely on reliability plots without ECE, Brier score, confidence intervals, or held-out calibration tuning.
Reviewer-identified: the split-data study is not a federated-learning or privacy evaluation and remains far below the ensemble and full-data accuracy.
Reviewer-identified: MergeMany has one small MNIST table and one selected 32-model calibration plot; later work shows pairwise methods can fail to place many models in one common basin.
Reviewer-identified: the NP-hardness reduction supports exact hardness, but its inapproximability conclusion is not approximation-preserving because of a large additive objective shift.
Reviewer-identified: the termination proof omits tied assignment updates, and MergeMany termination receives only an assertion rather than a separate global-potential proof.

Reviewer-identified: models must have identical structures and manually authored permutation specifications; depthwise/grouped convolutions, attention heads, and heterogeneous architectures are not generally supported.
Reviewer-identified: the core experiments predate modern transformers and foundation models; the paper itself tests only MLPs and image classifiers up to ResNet50.
Reviewer-identified: lower test loss after merging is sometimes described as better out-of-distribution performance even when the test set is the ordinary same-benchmark holdout.
Reviewer-identified: the repository is code-rich but documentation-poor and depends heavily on externally hosted W&B artifacts rather than a self-contained reproduction bundle.
failure_modes: Thin networks retain barriers even after the best reported matching method.
Very early checkpoints do not exhibit the alignment found at the end of training.
A locally optimal sequence of Hungarian updates can miss a task-optimal global permutation.
Tied assignment optima make the theoretical coordinate-descent transition rule ambiguous.
BatchNorm activation variance collapses under raw averaging unless moments are repaired from data.
GroupNorm and depthwise convolution constrain or remove channel permutations needed by the method.
Activation matching degrades when the matching sample is small, shifted, private, or unrepresentative.
Weight matching can align parameter geometry while ignoring units' functional importance on the target distribution.
Straight-through matching is computationally expensive and can inherit biased gradients from discrete projection.
Pairwise-good alignments can be mutually inconsistent across three or more models.
The aligned average can improve cross-entropy while degrading top-1 accuracy.
Split-data merging can look better in loss or calibration while remaining operationally much worse than ensembling.
Functionally equivalent models related by scaling, sign, rotation, or non-permutation symmetries may remain far apart after channel matching.
Arbitrary non-SGD solutions can remain separated under every possible permutation, as the paper's own counterexample shows.
A changed optimizer or learning rate can select endpoints with substantially different alignability.
External W&B artifacts or an old JAX/Nix environment can become unavailable or difficult to reproduce.

competitive_landscape.title: The Role of Permutation Invariance in Linear Mode Connectivity of Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Entezari et al. formulate the permutation-invariance conjecture and supply initial statistical and small-network evidence. Git Re-Basin's main advance is to construct fast explicit witnesses for larger convolutional and residual models, while also giving a finite counterexample to any unrestricted version.
competitive_landscape.source_version: ICLR 2022 conference paper, OpenReview forum dNigytemkL

competitive_landscape.title: Optimizing Mode Connectivity via Neuron Alignment
competitive_landscape.difference: Tatro et al. already combine activation-based neuron alignment with learned nonlinear connecting curves. Git Re-Basin derives a simple least-squares activation assignment but focuses on straight linear segments, introduces data-free bidirectional weight matching, and scales the analysis to widened ResNets.

competitive_landscape.title: Model Fusion via Optimal Transport
competitive_landscape.difference: Singh and Jaggi already align and fuse network units with hard or soft optimal transport across widths and non-IID data. Git Re-Basin jointly revisits layer permutations from both adjacent sides, supports residual and normalization constraints, and reports stronger results on the authors' selected VGG11 and ImageNet comparisons.

competitive_landscape.title: REPAIR: REnormalizing Permuted Activations for Interpolation Repair
competitive_landscape.difference: Jordan et al. show that even correctly aligned networks can suffer activation-variance collapse under averaging and repair layer moments. This supplies a mechanism for residual barriers that Git Re-Basin's permutation search cannot solve, and the reviewed paper's final ImageNet version adopts BatchNorm-statistic recalculation after publication.
competitive_landscape.source_version: ICLR 2023 conference paper, OpenReview forum gU5sJ6ZggcX

competitive_landscape.title: Re-Basin via Implicit Sinkhorn Differentiation
competitive_landscape.difference: Pena et al. replace discrete Hungarian projection with a differentiable Sinkhorn re-basin module optimized for a task-specific objective and demonstrate continual learning. It directly targets suboptimal discrete search and integration into gradient-based pipelines, at the cost of soft relaxation and data/task dependence.

competitive_landscape.title: Analysis of Linear Mode Connectivity via Permutation-Based Weight Matching: With Insights into Other Permutation Search Methods
competitive_landscape.difference: Ito et al. find that weight matching does not work merely by shrinking total parameter distance; it aligns singular-vector directions associated with large singular values, preserving dominant functionality. This gives a spectral account missing from Git Re-Basin and compares weight, activation, and straight-through matching for multi-model use.
competitive_landscape.source_version: ICLR 2025 conference paper, corresponding to arXiv:2402.04051v5

competitive_landscape.title: Analyzing the Role of Permutation Invariance in Linear Mode Connectivity
competitive_landscape.difference: Zhan et al. prove a restricted quantitative width result for two-layer ReLU teacher-student models: the modulo-permutation barrier has double descent and decays as O(m^-1/2) when sufficiently wide, while learning-rate-induced sparsity changes the barrier. This turns two Git Re-Basin observations into a narrow theory rather than a universal landscape claim.

competitive_landscape.title: Linear Mode Connectivity between Multiple Models modulo Permutation Symmetries
competitive_landscape.difference: Ito et al. show that permutation methods designed for two endpoints can fail to place many models in one common convex low-loss basin, then introduce STE-MM and evaluate pairwise barriers, merged loss, and Hessian trace. This directly tests and qualifies Git Re-Basin's lightly evaluated MergeMany extension.

competitive_landscape.title: Robustness and Regularization in Hierarchical Re-Basin
competitive_landscape.difference: Franke et al. introduce hierarchical merging and report robustness gains as more models are merged, but also observe a substantially larger Re-Basin performance drop than the original paper. It is direct primary evidence that MergeMany behavior and endpoint quality are more fragile than the MNIST example suggests.

competitive_landscape.title: Do We Really Need Permutations? Impact of Model Width on Linear Mode Connectivity
competitive_landscape.difference: Ito et al. report that sufficient width can yield linear connectivity even without permutations when softmax temperature is calibrated, and explain it with layerwise exponentially weighted connectivity. This challenges the interpretation that Git Re-Basin's width trend is mainly about a richer set of useful permutations and identifies calibration as a missing control.
competitive_landscape.source_version: ICLR 2026 conference paper, OpenReview forum ll8GLAic7q

competitive_landscape.title: Scaling Linear Mode Connectivity and Merging to Billion Parameter Pretrained Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: Li and Shen jointly learn functionality-preserving transformations from both endpoints toward a shared path and scale the idea to ViT-L and billion-parameter pretrained language models. Their bidirectional, transformer-scale results extend far beyond Git Re-Basin's manually specified MLP/CNN/ResNet permutations, though modern LLM barriers remain small rather than universally zero.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: After accounting for hidden-unit permutations, SGD solutions often occupy nearly one basin; three alignment algorithms expose barrier-free linear paths and permit useful data-free model merging, including the first zero-barrier result for independently trained ResNets on CIFAR-10.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The central weight-matching algorithm is a simple, fast, architecture-aware contribution that advanced both model merging and empirical loss-landscape analysis. Activation matching and neuron alignment predate it, as do optimal-transport fusion and the permutation-invariance conjecture, but the bidirectional whole-model assignment objective, practical residual-network support, width/onset experiments, and explicit finite counterexample form a distinctive package. The strongest theoretical framing is not established: a handful of pairwise line segments do not prove one global basin, the approximation-hardness proof has a gap, and ImageNet uses data-dependent BatchNorm repair.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: This is a high-impact methods paper and an influential empirical demonstration, not a proof that deep-network loss landscapes have a single convex basin. Its durable contribution is the re-basing primitive: quotient known parameter symmetries before averaging or interpreting Euclidean geometry. Reuse the released weight matcher and the counterexample; describe zero-barrier and merging results with their exact architecture, width, endpoint-pair, normalization-repair, and metric conditions. Later primary work validates the basic direction while adding variance repair, multi-model objectives, spectral explanations, width-only counterpoints, and transformer-scale transformations.

reusable_insights: Canonicalize function-preserving parameter symmetries before using Euclidean distance, interpolation, or averaging in weight space.
Represent architecture symmetries explicitly as shared permutations over parameter axes, especially across residual branches and normalization tensors.
A coupled whole-network assignment can be optimized cheaply by exact layer-coordinate Hungarian steps even when the global discrete problem is hard.
Data-free weight matching is valuable when training examples are unavailable, but task loss must still be evaluated independently.
Separate the existence of a good permutation from the ability of a heuristic to find it.
Pairwise low-barrier paths do not imply a jointly convex basin for three or more endpoints.
Treat width, optimizer, learning rate, and training time as determinants of alignability, not incidental hyperparameters.
Always compare permutation alignment with moment repair; activation-variance collapse can masquerade as a distinct basin.
If normalization statistics are recomputed along a path, describe the result as a repaired or data-dependent path rather than a strict full-state linear interpolation.
Measure merged-model accuracy, cross-entropy, calibration, robustness, and resource cost separately; improvement in one can hide degradation in another.
For privacy or federated claims, evaluate leakage, client heterogeneity, communication, and resource-matched alternatives rather than relying on data-free matching alone.
Use repeated random endpoint pairs and report the distribution of barriers and merge failures, not only a representative curve.
A finite adversarial counterexample is useful for locating exactly which optimizer-bias assumption a landscape conjecture needs.
Approximation-hardness reductions must preserve approximation ratios; large additive shifts invalidate multiplicative conclusions.
Coordinate-descent termination proofs need explicit strict-improvement and tie-breaking semantics matching the implementation.
Publish a figure-to-command manifest and immutable local result bundle even when experiment logs live on an external service.
open_questions: For which architectures, optimizers, learning rates, and widths does a low-barrier permutation exist with high probability over endpoint pairs?
Can a tractable algorithm certify that no function-preserving permutation achieves a requested barrier threshold?
What global objective best makes pairwise permutations cycle-consistent across many models?
How much of the reported width effect remains after temperature calibration and activation-moment repair without any permutation?
Can permutation, sign, scaling, rotation, and cross-layer symmetries be optimized in one principled quotient-space framework?
Which functional or spectral quantity explains why raw parameter inner-product matching preserves task behavior?
Can the inapproximability statement for the sum of bilinear assignments be repaired with a gap-preserving nonnegative reduction?
What tie rule gives Algorithm 1 a clean finite-termination guarantee while preserving its empirical speed?
Does MergeMany monotonically improve an explicit global pairwise-alignment potential, and when does its final average retain accuracy?
How often do independently sampled endpoint pairs fail on the same architecture and training recipe used in the headline figures?
Can the third-party reproduction discrepancy be resolved with an immutable checkpoint and environment bundle tied to every paper figure?
How well does re-basing work under realistic non-IID federated clients, privacy attacks, heterogeneous architectures, and asynchronous updates?
Does lower merged cross-entropy translate into robustness or distribution-shift gains after accuracy and calibration are jointly controlled?
Can transformer-scale symmetry specifications cover attention heads, MLP channels, normalization, embeddings, and tensor-parallel sharding without manual engineering?
What is the right definition of a basin when evaluation includes data-dependent BatchNorm recalibration or other post-interpolation repairs?
Does SGD really select a connected quotient-space region, or do matching and repair merely build isolated pairwise shortcuts?
reviewer_notes: Read the exact pinned source end to end and independently verified the PDF and extracted-text SHA-256 values. The OpenReview identity is preserved, but its automated route currently redirects to a browser challenge; the pinned source override is official arXiv:2209.04836v6, whose title, authors, 29-page length, ICLR 2023 banner, and content match the conference paper. Main text occupies pages 1-10, references pages 11-18, and Appendix A pages 19-29. Rendered and visually inspected every page, including all 13 figures, 3 tables, 3 algorithms, equations 1-18, both lemmas, both constructed examples, every width/onset/interpolation/calibration plot, and the two proof appendices. Audited the author repository at public head ef40098257ab97243930eba737d6dcb8edd5863e: 31 commits, MIT license, JAX experiment scripts, a pinned Nix environment, external W&B artifacts, no release, no CI, no packaged test suite, and almost no run instructions. The W&B project URL resolves as of 2026-08-24, but checkpoints and logs are not bundled locally. Also inspected the public third-party one-click reproduction report; its negative result is recorded only as an artifact warning because it is not a peer-reviewed primary paper. Current direct primary predecessors, competitors, corrective papers, theory, multi-model work, and transformer-scale successors were checked through 2026-08-24. Confidence is very high in the source, visual, artifact, equation, scope, BatchNorm-path, table, and hardness-reduction audits; high in the tie-handling proof critique; and moderate about the general prevalence of the empirical phenomenon because the paper does not report repeated endpoint-pair statistics.
